questions.question: According to industry research cited in the course lectures, approximately how much does an individual technical customer support telephone call cost a software vendor when users encounter confusing interfaces?
options: Estimates range from $12 to $250 per call
Exactly $0.05 per call
More than $50,000 per call
Customer support calls have zero financial cost to the vendor
questions.explanation: As cited in Module 01 Slide 10: 'Calls to customer support are very expensive for the vendor: estimates range from $12 to $250 per call.' A well-designed, usable interface drastically reduces call center volumes, saving enterprises millions of dollars annually.

why_wrong.1: Staffed telephone support requires trained human technicians and telecom infrastructure, costing far more than five cents.
why_wrong.2: $50,000 is an absurd overestimation for a routine phone call.
why_wrong.3: Salaries, facilities, and phone lines represent major vendor overhead costs.

questions.question: The Association for Computing Machinery's Special Interest Group on Computer-Human Interaction (ACM SIGCHI) defines HCI as a discipline concerned with the {{c1::design}}, {{c2::evaluation}}, and {{c3::implementation}} of interactive computing systems for human use.
options: design
evaluation
implementation
fabrication
marketing
monetization
questions.explanation: The official ACM SIGCHI definition states: 'Human-Computer Interaction is a discipline concerned with the design, evaluation, and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use and with the study of the major phenomena surrounding them.'

questions.question: What is the technical term in usability engineering that describes how easily a first-time user can accomplish basic tasks the very first time they encounter an interactive interface?
questions.explanation: Learnability is the ease with which novices can understand and navigate an interface upon their initial exposure, without requiring formal training or extensive manuals.
marking_points: Identifies 'learnability' or 'ease of learning'.

questions.question: Conducting user research and usability testing before writing code actually reduces total software development and maintenance costs over the system lifecycle.
options: False — user research is a pure financial waste that always adds 50% overhead to project costs without benefit.

True — learning about users first prevents teams from building complex features users never use, and finding interface design defects during early requirements is up to 100 times cheaper than fixing them after software deployment.
questions.explanation: As taught in Module 01 Slide 8: 'Learn about users first, and you will avoid implementing features users don't want.' Software engineering economics (e.g. Boehm's cost-of-change curve) confirms that fixing usability mistakes after product rollout is vastly more expensive than discovering them during early user analysis.

why_wrong.0: User research saves substantial money by preventing re-coding of unwanted or flawed features.

questions.verified_output: True. Early user research reduces development and rework costs.

questions.question: In the student's handwritten lecture notes, the author of the primary recommended course textbook for INS 202 was noted as 'Gerard Kym'. What is the full, formal academic name of this textbook author?
questions.explanation: The textbook author is Dr. Gerard Jounghyun Kim, author of *Human-Computer Interaction: Fundamentals and Practice* (CRC Press), cited throughout the lecture slides and referenced in the student notebook.
marking_points: Identifies 'Gerard Jounghyun Kim' (or 'Gerard Kim').

questions.question: Which of the following describes a foundational characteristic of the User-Centered Development (UCD) methodology?
options: It is user-centric rather than data-centric, actively involves users throughout the design lifecycle, measures usability quantitatively, and is highly iterative.
It designs the complete software architecture in secret without ever showing drafts or prototypes to human users until product release.
It treats managers as the only users whose opinions matter, ignoring workers in the field.
It mandates that all applications must run exclusively on mechanical punched cards.
questions.explanation: As defined in Module 01 Slide 27: User-Centered Development is user-centric (not data-centric), involves real users in early stages, quantifies usability metrics, and operates iteratively through continuous prototype testing and refinement.

why_wrong.1: Designing in secret without user contact violates user-centered development.
why_wrong.2: Managers are not users; their assumptions often contradict actual user workflows.
why_wrong.3: UCD applies across modern graphical, touch, mobile, and web interfaces.

questions.verified_output: User-centric, iterative, measures usability with users.

questions.question:
[Case Scenario: Nile University deploys a new online Course Registration Portal for 8,000 undergraduate students. The portal database has full functional capability (Utility): ...]

Apply the HCI goals of 'Safety', 'Usability', and 'Efficiency' to propose three concrete interface improvements to resolve the registration portal's crises.
questions.answer: The university should implement: (1) Safety (Data Safety & Error Prevention): Introduce state persistence and auto-save so that hitting the browser Back button or experiencing an interrupted network session does not erase selected courses, and add a warning dialog before any destructive cancellation; (2) Usability (Error Recovery & Learnability): Replace the cryptic hex code 'FATAL EXCEPTION 0x80041002' with a clear, actionable human-language error message indicating the exact conflict (e.g., 'Timetable Clash: COS 201 at 10:00 AM overlaps with IFT 211. Please choose an alternative section'); (3) Efficiency & Visual Affordance: Redesign the 'Confirm & Submit' link as a prominent, high-contrast, primary action button placed directly below the course selection summary with a visible progress indicator.
questions.explanation: Applies Safety (state persistence), Usability (clear error messaging), and Efficiency (prominent submit button).
marking_points: Applies Safety: auto-saving course selections and preventing accidental data wiping on Back button.
Applies Usability: translating cryptic hex codes into clear, actionable human language identifying the conflicting courses.
Applies Efficiency: converting tiny hidden text links into a prominent, high-contrast submit button with progress indicators.
Shows how these improvements restore student registration completion rates.
questions.verified_output: Safety, Usability, and Efficiency redesign proposals.

questions.question:
[Case Scenario: A fast-growing fintech startup in Lagos launches a peer-to-peer mobile payments app. In version 1.0, to send money to a friend, the user must navigate through 6...]

Analyze how the introduction of contact book syncing and the 'Favorites' carousel improved both 'Efficiency' and 'Usability' (specifically memory load) in version 2.0.
questions.answer: In version 1.0, requiring users to recall and manually type 10-digit account numbers and bank codes placed heavy cognitive strain on human short-term memory (violating George Miller's $7 \pm 2$ limit) and created extreme friction. Version 2.0 improved Usability by replacing 'recall' with 'recognition': users simply recognize a friend's familiar name or profile picture in their synced contact list. Version 2.0 dramatically improved Efficiency by reducing the multi-step navigation from 6 cumbersome screens down to a 2-tap workflow (tapping the Favorite avatar and confirming via biometrics), reducing task completion time from 90 seconds to under 4 seconds while virtually eliminating costly typographical transfer errors.
questions.explanation: Replaces recall with recognition, cuts task time from 90s to 4s, and eliminates memory overload.
marking_points: Identifies that manual typing placed heavy load on limited short-term memory.
Explains how contact syncing replaces difficult 'recall' with effortless 'recognition'.
Shows that the 'Favorites' carousel elevates Efficiency by slashing screens, clicks, and transaction time.
Notes the sharp reduction in user transfer errors and call center volume.
questions.verified_output: Efficiency and Usability analysis (recognition vs recall).

questions.question: Match each Gestalt visual perception principle to its defining user interface application:
options: Proximity
Similarity
Continuity / Alignment
Closure

answer.Proximity: Placing input field text labels significantly closer to their corresponding form boxes than to preceding fields so users perceive them as a pair.
answer.Similarity: Rendering all clickable primary action buttons in the identical blue pill shape and font across every screen to indicate common functionality.
answer.Continuity / Alignment: Left-aligning all headings, paragraph text, and input boxes along a single vertical axis to facilitate smooth, rapid top-to-bottom visual scanning.
answer.Closure: Designing an icon or logo using broken or striped lines (like the IBM logo) where the mind automatically fills in the blanks to see complete letters.

questions.explanation: Proximity groups by physical distance; Similarity groups by shared visual attributes (color, shape); Continuity aligns along virtual visual axes; Closure mentally connects incomplete outlines.

pairs.right: Placing input field text labels significantly closer to their corresponding form boxes than to preceding fields so users perceive them as a pair.
Rendering all clickable primary action buttons in the identical blue pill shape and font across every screen to indicate common functionality.
Left-aligning all headings, paragraph text, and input boxes along a single vertical axis to facilitate smooth, rapid top-to-bottom visual scanning.
Designing an icon or logo using broken or striped lines (like the IBM logo) where the mind automatically fills in the blanks to see complete letters.

questions.question: According to Fitts's Law, the time required to move a cursor or finger to an interactive target is governed by which mathematical relationship?
options: Target movement time increases with greater Distance (D) to the target and decreases with greater Target Width (W): T = a + b * log2(1 + D/W)
Target movement time is equal to the CPU clock frequency multiplied by the RAM bus width
Target movement time is completely independent of button size or distance
Target movement time decreases when the button is made infinitely tiny
questions.explanation: Fitts's Law states: $T = a + b \log_2(1 + D/W)$. Movement time increases as the target distance ($D$) increases, and decreases as the target size/width ($W$) increases. Making buttons larger and closer reduces acquisition time and user errors.

why_wrong.1: Fitts's Law is a human biomechanical model of hand/eye movement, not a CPU hardware metric.
why_wrong.2: Decades of empirical psychology prove that target distance and width directly dictate movement speed.
why_wrong.3: Tiny buttons are difficult to click, causing massive acquisition delays and mis-clicks.

questions.source: Fitts's Law; Ergonomics Literature; Gerard Kim Text

questions.question: The cognitive practice of organizing long strings of data into smaller, meaningful groups to ease short-term memory burden is called {{c1::chunking}}. For instance, the 10-digit sequence 0803314492 is easier to remember when formatted as {{c2::080-331-4492}}.
options: chunking
formatting
paging
defragmenting
hashing
questions.explanation: Chunking transforms unmanageable raw sequences into familiar units within George Miller's $7 \pm 2$ capacity limit (e.g. breaking a 10-digit phone number into three distinct 3-to-4-digit chunks).

questions.question: A user looking at an ambiguous black-and-white visual figure sees either the letter 'B' or the number '13'. If the symbol is placed between '12' and '14', the user instantly reads '13'. What cognitive phenomenon does this demonstrate?
options: The dominant role of Context and Mindset in human visual perception
A catastrophic bit-flip in the user's sensory registers
Failure of the monitor's refresh rate to sync with room lighting
The mathematical Consensus theorem of Boolean algebra
questions.explanation: As highlighted in Module 02 Slides 8–15: Context and mindset play a major role in what people perceive. The exact same visual stimuli are interpreted completely differently depending on the surrounding environmental context.

why_wrong.1: Humans do not experience electronic hardware register bit-flips.
why_wrong.2: Perceptual ambiguity is cognitive, not monitor refresh flicker.
why_wrong.3: Consensus theorem simplifies Boolean logic gates, not psychological reading context.

questions.question: Which Gestalt psychology law states that elements that are placed physically close together in visual space are perceived by the human visual system as belonging to a unified, coherent group?
questions.explanation: The Law of Proximity states that objects placed in close spatial proximity are perceived as a collective group, dominating other visual attributes like color or shape.
marking_points: Identifies 'Proximity' (or 'Law of Proximity').
